cim: What Artificial Intelligence (AI) research misses about African markets (By Bas Wijne)
cim_eredeti: What Artificial Intelligence (AI) research misses about African markets (By Bas Wijne)
szoveg_eredeti:
By Bas Wijne, CEO at APO Group (www.APO-opa.com).

Your company has bid to supply a manufacturer in Côte d’Ivoire, and the proposal reaches a procurement lead in Abidjan. She hasn't heard of you. Before she replies, she asks ChatGPT or another AI assistant, in French, who you are and whether you’ve worked in the country.

The assistant builds its answer from what has been published about you online. If you’ve only just entered the market, that might be a single local article or a two-year-old announcement. Whatever it finds becomes her first impression of you.

That impression depends on which local websites the assistant is allowed to read, and on the language she asks in. Yet most advice on preparing for that moment rests on research from outside Africa. The Reuters Institute’s widely quoted 2023 count of news sites that stop AI companies collecting their pages covered 10 countries, none of them African. The same institute now finds African markets among those driving growth in AI use for news.

APO Group (www.APO-opa.com) can see some of what that research misses. We are a communications consultancy that owns its distribution: a pan-African newswire, Africa Newsroom (https://www.Africa-Newsroom.com/), which reaches more than 250 Africa-focused news sites. Crawlers, the programs AI companies use to collect pages for live answers or future training, visit Africa Newsroom around 200,000 times a day. Microsoft’s AI services, including Copilot, name an Africa Newsroom page as a source about 16,000 times a month; and Google AI, including AI overviews and search, draws about 62,000 impressions a month.

The answer draws on everything an assistant can read

In August and September, we asked six AI assistants about 16 of our recent announcements more than 400 times, in four languages used across the continent. Their answers included the news in 90% of tests and named or linked to Africa Newsroom as the source in 25%. When they credited someone else, it was often the company’s own website or another news outlet. Answers to questions in French, Portuguese and Arabic included the news almost as often as those in English.

African news outlets are also primed for AI search. In the US and UK, 79% of the biggest news sites block at least one AI crawler, according to BuzzStream. In South Africa, GIBS business school’s Media Leadership Think Tank found that 30% of 263 news sites do, mostly large publishers with the resources to block. Across websites of every kind in Nigeria, Kenya, Côte d’Ivoire and Senegal, the web-data company Zyte found just 12% to 14% do.

Publishers that block AI have a fair case: assistants answer questions using their journalism, so fewer readers visit them as the primary source. A company announcing news has the opposite challenge: its announcement exists to be found. In these markets, being found depends on relationships with local news outlets in each country.

The industry calls the work of being found and credited by AI assistants generative engine optimisation, or GEO.

Our media monitoring reports show clients when AI assistants, including ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity and DeepSeek, name their Africa Newsroom announcements as a source. Then we advise them on how to be cited more often.

Hundreds of companies will bring their news to Africa Tech Festival this week. Far more of the questions their news answers will be asked after the event ends, by people who weren’t in the room. One of them may be a procurement lead in Abidjan, asking in French about a company she's never heard of. When she asks about you, the assistant will answer from whatever has already been written. The only open question is who wrote it.

Bas Wijne speaks on Beyond the Copilot: Orchestrating Multi-Agent Systems Across the Enterprise at Africa Tech Festival in Cape Town, alongside Sabine Dall’Omo, CEO of Siemens Sub-Saharan Africa; Strini Mudaly, CIO of Gold Fields; Shafee Khan of Microsoft; and Victoria Evdokimova of Yango.

About APO Group: Founded in 2007 by Nicolas Pompigne-Mognard, APO Group is the communications consultancy built for performance, combining strategic advisory, on-the-ground execution, and guaranteed visibility across all 54 African markets. Its owned newswire, Africa Newsroom, secures placement on 250+ Africa-focused news sites, connecting organisations directly with 450,000+ journalists, analysts, investors, and policymakers worldwide.

Recognised internationally for communications excellence, including SABRE, Davos Communications, and World Business Outlook distinctions, APO Group partners with global and African organisations for whom the continent is a strategic priority. Clients include the African Development Bank Group, Africa CDC, Afreximbank, NFL, Nestlé, Emirates, Canon, Western Union and GITEX Global.
